title: Kara: the steel circle
hookLine: a steel bracelet, a circle without end, reminding the hand what it's for

lines: A STEEL CIRCLE AT THE WRIST.
cards: Some people tie a string around a finger so they won't forget something. Others write a word on the back of their hand. The trick works because hands are always in view: typing, reaching, holding a cup, holding a phone.
Want a reminder you'll see a hundred times a day? Put it on your hand. Sikhs keep one there too: a plain circle of steel at the wrist.
Today, the third of the five Ks: kara.

teach.b: Kara means a bracelet, and the Sikh kara is a very particular one: plain steel or iron, no gold, no gems, no decoration. It's worn on the wrist, often the right, or the hand a person uses most.
It carries three simple ideas. First, the circle.

teach.h: A CIRCLE: NO BEGINNING, NO END.
teach.b: It has no beginning and no end, and Sikhs often say that's a picture of God, the One without beginning or end, and of the unbroken bond between a Sikh and the Guru. Second, the steel.
Not gold, which says wealth, or silver, which says status.

teach.h: STEEL: HUMBLE, STRONG, THE SAME FOR ALL.
teach.b: Steel is what tools and plows are made of, humble and strong. Rich or poor, a Sikh wears the same kara.
Third, the one people remember: the hand. Every time the hand moves, the kara moves with it.
Reaching for something that isn't yours, raising a fist in anger, signing a dishonest paper: the steel is right there, catching the light, asking a quiet question.
What are these hands doing? It's the same question under the whole rehat. The Gurus taught kirat karni, honest work with your own hands, and seva, service with your own hands.
The kara just keeps the question on your wrist. You'll often see it on Sikhs who don't keep all five, and on Punjabi wrists of other backgrounds too.
Plain, heavy, cool against the skin, and never quite letting you forget.

how: Sikhs who keep the five Ks wear a plain steel or iron kara on the wrist, and other Sikhs often wear one too, as a constant reminder of the Guru and of what their hands should do.

o: a steel ring worn on the finger for luck
a gold bangle given as a wedding gift
a plain steel bracelet worn at the wrist

games.q: the kara, turned three ways — tap the pairs.
p: humble, strong, the same for all
honest work with your own hands

s: a gold kara is a finer way to keep the rehat
the kara is plain steel or iron: the same for rich and poor.
Sikhs who don't keep all five Ks sometimes still wear a kara
it's a K you'll often see on wrists that carry no other.
the kara is meant as decoration
it's a reminder: the circle of God and the Guru, and a question for the hand.

games.q: you're angry and your hand starts to rise. in the kara's picture, what happens?
o: the kara is just jewelry; nothing.
the steel at the wrist moves with the hand, asking what these hands are doing.
the kara means you should strike first.
games.why: every movement of the hand carries the kara with it, a quiet question on the wrist.

practice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and look at them. Think of what they've done today, what they carried, typed, cooked, held, maybe what they shouldn't have done, with honest looking and no scolding.
Then choose one good thing these hands will do before the day ends, and let them rest, open, while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Kara. The plain steel bracelet, the third K: a circle without end, the same for rich and poor, reminding the hand what it's for.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kara, the steel bracelet; the ੜ is a flapped r, made with a quick flick of the tongue.

carryVoice: Your line: what are these hands doing. The steel asks; the hands answer. That's day two hundred sixty-seven.
